title: Managing Critical State: Distributed Consensus for Reliability
subtitle: Use proven agreement protocols to preserve critical state
summary: Pip’s booking coordinator splits across a network partition. Preserving one agreed critical state may require some nodes to stop accepting work. Consensus, ordered operations, stable leadership, and carefully placed quorums make that trade-off explicit.

concepts.title: CAP, safety, and availability
concepts.body: Pip’s minority partition wants to assign its own lock owner. During a partition, serving every node conflicts with one consistent view of critical state. Consensus preserves safety by refusing conflicting commits, potentially pausing without a quorum; liveness concerns eventual progress. Pip still needs eventual communication and redundancy because an asynchronous network cannot guarantee bounded progress.

concepts.title: Replicated state machines and ordered operations
concepts.body: Pip gives replicas the same balance updates in different orders and gets different outcomes. A replicated state machine needs deterministic operations applied in the same agreed order. Consensus establishes that order; missed decisions need catch-up. Pip also defines reads: any replica may be stale, while strong reads need a mechanism establishing currentness.

concepts.title: Paxos and stable-leader Multi-Paxos
concepts.body: Pip’s coordinator uses numbered proposals, persistent acceptor commitments, and overlapping majorities. Paxos preserves prior accepted decisions as proposals advance; a higher-level log orders repeated agreements. Stable-leader Multi-Paxos reuses established leadership for normal operations. Pip monitors elections, randomized backoff, and competing proposers because safe decisions alone do not ensure timely progress.

concepts.title: Quorum placement and operational trade-offs
concepts.body: Pip places five replicas across independent sites. Three communicating survivors can tolerate two unavailable replicas if they have capacity. Distance and losing a fast quorum member can increase latency; a leader may bottleneck bandwidth. Pip tracks health, lag, leadership changes, and committed progress instead of equating running processes with a functioning consensus service.

misconceptions.claim: A missed heartbeat proves the old leader has stopped writing.
misconceptions.correction: A timeout can indicate a partition or delay; safe leadership needs a proven agreement mechanism and its enforced ownership rules.

misconceptions.claim: Adding one replica always improves availability.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing a majority group from five to six raises the quorum from three to four without increasing the number of tolerated failures.

scenario.title: Choose coordination for critical state
scenario.context: A leader election service loses a node during a zone network partition. Clients must avoid two writers accepting conflicting configuration.

options.label: Use a consensus protocol with explicit failure assumptions
options.benefit: A quorum rule protects consistency during node loss.
options.cost: Unavailable writes are a deliberate availability cost.
options.consequence: The system rejects writes without quorum and repairs membership after the partition.

options.label: Let each zone continue writing independently
options.benefit: Each zone keeps serving without waiting for quorum.
options.cost: Divergent state requires difficult reconciliation and may corrupt consumers.
options.consequence: Both zones progress, then disagree about the authoritative value.

scenario.debrief: Preserving one configuration history requires a quorum and safe leadership, not independent writers in each partition. The side without a quorum pauses writes; restored replicas catch up before participating normally.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a replicated state machine from replicas merely receiving the same operations?
options: Each replica may choose any execution order
Replicas must finish each operation at exactly the same wall-clock time
They execute deterministic operations in the same agreed order
quiz.explanation: Order is part of the state-machine guarantee; different orders can produce different results.

quiz.question: What is the normal-case benefit of a stable Multi-Paxos leader?
options: It removes durable logging from acceptors after the leader is elected
It avoids repeating the preparation phase for every operation
It lets the leader commit without a majority while its process is healthy
quiz.explanation: Established leadership reduces coordination while retaining quorum-based acceptance.

quiz.question: A five-replica majority group loses contact with three replicas. What is the safe default for new commits?
options: Pause because the remaining two cannot form a quorum
Commit locally and reconcile conflicting ownership later
Treat an operator’s timeout as proof the missing replicas are empty
quiz.explanation: Without a quorum, the survivors cannot safely establish new decisions under the existing membership.

exercise.title: Place a consensus quorum
exercise.prompt: Plan a five-replica configuration service across failure domains. Explain which failures preserve progress and what clients observe when no quorum is reachable.

fields.label: Placement
